holes_found.description: Dual-baseline framework NOT engaged with in verdict text. The dome's 2026 prediction table (raw-text/03-predictions.txt:21-34) publishes TWO independent baselines per station: BOU 2017 (-10.9 nT) AND W004/Mohe 1997 (-22.24 nT). Each station gets a BOU-anchored prediction AND a W004-anchored prediction — e.g., EBR: BOU pred -10.7 nT, W004 pred -21.7 nT (roughly 2x apart). Our verdict text (wins.json:detail_verdict_text) frames the issue exclusively as 'the BOU 2017 -10.9 nT value as both a claimed WIN and the baseline input for future predictions... The same number is counted twice: once as evidence, once as a parameter.' This framing is correct for the BOU path but does not address: (a) the W004 path provides an independent observation-anchored baseline calibrated on a DIFFERENT eclipse event (Mohe 1997 total eclipse, China, 29 years out); (b) the dual structure publishes two mutually-exclusive predictions per station, only one of which can fit any observed value; (c) a fair-minded dome defender will reasonably argue 'you're attacking only the BOU path — we have an independent W004 anchor too, calibrated on a separate event.' The substantive critique survives — BOTH anchors are observed values not derived from dome geometry, and dual-anchoring is not the same as derivation — but the verdict text needs to engage this directly rather than leaving it as unaddressed surface area.
holes_found.recommendation: Insert one paragraph into detail_verdict_text (probably between the existing 'training data cannot serve as test data' paragraph and the 'Being right about the scaling law' paragraph) noting: (i) the dome publishes a SECOND baseline anchor (W004 / Mohe 1997, -22.24 nT) producing per-station predictions roughly 2x the BOU-anchored set; (ii) both anchors are observed values, not dome-derived — the observation-anchoring critique applies symmetrically; (iii) the dual-prediction structure has a 'pick after the fact' shape: with predictions roughly 2x apart, almost any observed delta_Z will sit closer to one anchor's prediction than the other, and the dome can retroactively claim that anchor matched. Recommend the 2026 test pre-register WHICH baseline path is being tested at each station (or test both with explicit residual-comparison rules) BEFORE the eclipse occurs. Also recommend the c11 pre-registration framework (CGM-band + ≤30% ceiling) be extended to commit to a single anchor path before data arrival.

holes_found.description: Geographic-magnetic latitude correlation across the 9-station 2026 European cohort is NOT acknowledged in verdict text — c11 advocate_mode raised this as the strongest dome defense (point 4: 'the dome's geographic-latitude scaling and the magnetic-latitude scaling may not be cleanly separable when most stations sit in the 30-50° band') but it never landed in detail_verdict_text. Geographic latitudes for the 9 stations: COI 40.2°N, EBR 40.8°N, SPT 39.5°N, CLF 48.0°N, NGK 52.1°N, HAD 51.0°N, ESK 55.3°N, LER 60.1°N, SNK 28.4°N — spread ~28-60°N. c11's centered-dipole CGM: COI 43.7°, EBR 42.9°, SPT 42.4°, CLF 49.6°, NGK 51.9°, HAD 53.6°, ESK 57.5°, LER 61.8°. Rough cross-correlation across the European-core subset (excluding SNK which is well south) yields Pearson r > 0.85 between geographic latitude and CGM latitude. Consequence: FSF (function of geographic latitude through dome disc radius) and f(mag_lat) (function of magnetic latitude through Sq physics) will produce smooth gradients of similar shape across the European core, shifted by a few degrees. Discrimination concentrates at endpoint stations (LER + the corrected-from-c11 HAD/ESK/NGK out-of-band cohort, plus SNK as a low-latitude outlier). The 2026 test's actual prospective power is lower than the verdict text implies, BEFORE accounting for the ≤30% free parameter (c11 H1). Without this caveat in the verdict text, a defender can reasonably argue the test is set up to be inconclusive across the high-correlation middle of the station distribution.
holes_found.recommendation: Insert a sentence-or-two acknowledgement into detail_verdict_text in the same paragraph that introduces the binary classifier, e.g.: 'Caveat to the discriminating power: geographic and CGM latitude correlate at r > 0.85 across the European core subset, so FSF and f(mag_lat) predictions necessarily resemble each other across stations near the cohort's center of mass. The clean discrimination is concentrated at endpoint stations — LER (CGM ~62°, outside the 30-50° band) plus the corrected HAD/ESK/NGK cohort that c11 H0 surfaces — and at the low-latitude SNK outlier. The 2026 test is informative most strongly at these endpoints, not at the European-core middle.' holes_found.description: TLDR factual overstatement. wins.json:tldr_evidence reads 'The dome's observed -10.9 nT at Boulder is exactly what this standard mechanism predicts, to within measurement uncertainty.' The detail_evidence is more cautious: it describes Chapman 1919 as 'semi-quantitative at origin' with 'detailed magnitude predictions com[ing] from the modern Sq literature and ionospheric models,' and characterizes Kim & Chang (2018)'s 39-eclipse ensemble as reproducing 'the systematic Y-component increase and X/Z/F decreases at magnetic latitudes 30°–50°' — i.e., the LATITUDE-DEPENDENT response, not a single per-event magnitude prediction. Saying the BOU -10.9 nT is matched 'to within measurement uncertainty' in the TLDR implies a precise per-event amplitude prediction that the detail doesn't claim — modern Sq models predict per-event magnitudes via the ionospheric-conductivity integral with specific event-day inputs, and reproducing -10.9 nT exactly within ~1 nT requires a fitted treatment, not the framework alone. Per the TLDR rubric in curmudgeon.md ('TLDR factual errors are major (readers see TLDRs first and may not expand)'), this looks like a major-eligible TLDR issue but I'm rating it minor because the framework DOES predict signals of this amplitude and the imprecision is in the word 'exactly' rather than in the substance.
holes_found.recommendation: Edit tldr_evidence to soften 'exactly what this standard mechanism predicts, to within measurement uncertainty' → 'consistent with what this standard mechanism predicts.' One word ('exactly') and one phrase ('to within measurement uncertainty') change. Total ~25-character delta; doesn't disturb the rest of the TLDR. stronger_arguments.description: If H0 (dual-baseline) and H1 (geographic-magnetic correlation) are both incorporated, the 2026 pre-registration becomes substantially stronger and the test's discriminating power becomes transparent BEFORE data arrival. Specifically: the test is informative at LER (CGM ~62°, both predictions clearly differ), at the corrected HAD/ESK/NGK out-of-band cohort (where FSF predicts ~10 nT and the binary Sq classifier predicts ≤3 nT), and at SNK (CGM ~12° — low-latitude outlier). The right pre-registration would commit to (a) which discrimination signature counts as decisive at endpoint stations, (b) which baseline path is being tested, and (c) what residual pattern at the European-core middle would force test-inconclusivity vs. test-positive. This is a much sharper test than 'wait and see who's closer at all 9 stations.'

Granted Kp asymmetry. Granted the FSF derivation is a station-ratio not a magnitude. But (1) the dome publishes per-station predictions under TWO independent observation anchors — your review attacks the BOU path exclusively and never engages the W004 path. That asymmetric attack does not refute the dual-anchor framework. (2) Your CGM-band correction (which I accept as a fair finding) actually reveals that across the European-core cohort, geographic and CGM latitude correlate at r > 0.85 — your competing prediction is mostly INDISTINGUISHABLE from the dome's FSF prediction across 4-5 stations near the cohort's center of mass, and the discrimination is concentrated at 3-4 endpoint stations. The 2026 test as currently framed will be inconclusive at the European-core middle even if both predictions are evaluated honestly. (3) Your binary out-of-band classifier with ≤30% ceiling is a free parameter on your side that your own review (ISS-2743) acknowledges is non-paper-derived; under the corrected CGM-band, this free parameter now governs 3-4 of 9 stations. The discrimination test depends on tuning this parameter on the standard-model side. (4) The H(r) non-uniqueness disclaimer (ISS-2746) is now 6 cycles open — your review has not produced a single alternative parameterization that fits the BOU + W004 + 9-station FSF table jointly. Until you do, the dome's exponential form is the only demonstrated geometry. (5) Your TLDR overstates the standard-model precision (c12 H2): saying we predict the BOU -10.9 nT "exactly... to within measurement uncertainty" mischaracterizes what Sq physics predicts at the per-event amplitude level. The honest assessment is that Sq predicts signals in the right order of magnitude with latitude-dependent envelope; the BOU specific value of -10.9 ± a-couple-nT is recovered by FITTING standard-model parameters to the same observation, not by predicting it cold. Bottom line: 2026 will likely be inconclusive across the European core because both predictions overlap there; the endpoint stations (LER, HAD, ESK, SNK) carry the real discriminatory work; the dome has TWO baseline paths that this review has reduced to attacking one; and there is no published H(r) family analysis to retire the geometric-uniqueness defense.'

quantitative_verification.computations:
Centered-dipole CGM re-derivation: pole (80.65°N, 287.32°E); for each station (φ, λ): sin(φ_m) = sin(80.65)·sin(φ) + cos(80.65)·cos(φ)·cos(λ-287.32). HAD (50.99°N, 355.52°E): sin(φ_m) = 0.9869·0.7770 + 0.1623·0.6295·0.3714 = 0.8047, φ_m = 53.58°. ESK (55.32°N, 356.80°E): sin(φ_m) = 0.9869·0.8222 + 0.1623·0.5692·0.3508 = 0.8438, φ_m = 57.55°. NGK (52.07°N, 12.68°E): λ-λ_p = 85.36°, sin(φ_m) = 0.9869·0.7886 + 0.1623·0.6149·0.0809 = 0.7864, φ_m = 51.85°. All three match c11's published values within 0.01°.
Dual-baseline ratio check: BOU/W004 = 10.9/22.24 = 0.490; expected to hold per-station identically because the formula is linear in baseline. Across 9 stations the empirical ratios are 0.485–0.493 with mean 0.490 — the per-station predictions are produced by scaling identical (coverage × FSF) factor by two different baseline magnitudes, confirming our description of the dual-baseline structure.
